spec.description: The July 2019 heat wave on New York's streets, hour by hour, from 354 sensors on street trees and light poles in the neighbourhoods most at risk; every building coloured by the air around it (Kepler Plus Buildings layer).

options.content:
### Where the data comes from

In the summers of 2018 and 2019, as part of the [Cool Neighborhoods NYC](https://www.nyc.gov/site/orr/challenges/cool-neighborhoods.page) initiative, NYC Parks, the Mayor's Office of Resilience and the Department of Health hung small temperature sensors on street trees and light poles, block by block, in the neighbourhoods with the highest heat mortality risk: East Harlem, the South Bronx, Brownsville and others. Their hourly means are published as [Hyperlocal Temperature Monitoring](https://data.cityofnewyork.us/Environment/Hyperlocal-Temperature-Monitoring/qdq3-9eqn) on NYC Open Data. This dashboard keeps the ten days around the July 2019 heat wave, 15 to 24 July (354 sensors, 84,595 hours), in °C; the neighbourhoods are the city's 2010 Neighborhood Tabulation Areas.

### How to read the map

- The buildings are OpenStreetMap's, from the base map's own tiles, at their mapped height (5 m where none is mapped). Each is coloured by the air temperature **estimated at its centre** from the closest sensors (inverse distance weighting, power 2, the 12 closest), the same estimate a Surface layer draws between sensors.
- It is the **street air around the building**, not the building itself: the sensors hang about 3 m up in the street. Its roof and its rooms can be far hotter or cooler.
- A building more than 250 m from every sensor is grey: no estimate is made that far out.
- Hover a building for its card: the same estimate at that building, hour by hour over the ten days, the brushed hour as its value. A click on the card's pin keeps it while you look at another.
- The classes are the same for every hour and every neighbourhood, in °C: below 24, then every 2 degrees, then 40 and above. The heat wave's nights stayed at 28 to 30 °C in East Harlem.

### The two maps below

- **Heat vulnerability**: the Health Department's [Heat Vulnerability Index](https://data.cityofnewyork.us/Health/Heat-Vulnerability-Index-Rankings/4mhf-duep) by ZIP code, from 1 (lowest risk) to 5 (highest), on every building of the ZIP code. East Harlem's ZIP codes are at 4 and 5; the Upper East Side's, just south of them, at 1.
- **By hexagon**: the sensors averaged per H3 hexagon (resolution 9, about 0.1 km²) by DuckDB on the server, and each building given its hexagon's mean. The same data as the first map, binned instead of interpolated.

### What the sensors say

Over the ten days' afternoons (12 to 17 h), the 102 sensors on light poles read 1.8 °C more than the 252 in street trees (33.1 against 31.3 °C on average; 40.2 against 37.6 °C at 15:00 on the 21st); at night the two are within half a degree. Part of it is a tree's shade, part where each kind of sensor stands: the table and the map show which blocks.

The hottest hour in East Harlem was 15:00 on Sunday 21 July 2019: a mean of 37.1 °C over its sensors, and 34.8 to 44.6 °C from one block to another.

spec.rawSql:
-- The neighbourhood hour by hour: the mean of its sensors in bars, the hottest one as a line.
-- A picture to brush over: the window it writes (t0, t1) is the hour the map shows.
SELECT time, round(avg(temp_c), 1) AS "Mean of the sensors", max(temp_c) AS "Hottest sensor"
FROM 'http://feeds/datasets/nyc-street-heat/readings.parquet'
WHERE nta = ${nta:sqlstring}
GROUP BY time ORDER BY time

spec.description: The hour the map shows: bars are the neighbourhood's mean, the line its hottest sensor. Drag the window, step it hour by hour or press play: the buildings, the cards and the table follow. Scrolled out of view, it stays at the top.
spec.title: Hours on the map

spec.rawSql:
-- The neighbourhood's sensors averaged per H3 hexagon (resolution 9, about 0.1 km²) for every hour, each mean at
-- the middle of its hour. The map's time filter keeps the brushed window; a building's card charts its hexagon's
-- ten days.
SELECT h3_h3_to_string(h3_latlng_to_cell(latitude, longitude, 9)) AS h3,
       time + INTERVAL 30 MINUTE AS time,
       round(avg(temp_c), 1) AS temp_c, count(DISTINCT sensor) AS sensors
FROM 'http://feeds/datasets/nyc-street-heat/readings.parquet'
WHERE nta = ${nta:sqlstring}
GROUP BY 1, 2
ORDER BY 2

spec.description: The same sensors as the map above, averaged per H3 hexagon of about 0.1 km² on the server, and every building coloured by its hexagon's mean in the brushed hour: blocky where the map above is smooth. A building in a hexagon with no sensor stays grey. Hover a building for its hexagon's ten days.
spec.title: The sensors by hexagon, in the brushed hour

config.label: Air temperature, mean of the hexagon's sensors (°C)

spec.rawSql:
-- The ZIP codes round the neighbourhood's sensors, each with its Heat Vulnerability Index (DOHMH: 1 lowest
-- risk, 5 highest). The Buildings layer gives every building the index of the ZIP code it stands in.
WITH s AS (
  SELECT min(latitude) AS s, max(latitude) AS n, min(longitude) AS w, max(longitude) AS e
  FROM 'http://feeds/datasets/nyc-street-heat/readings.parquet' WHERE nta = ${nta:sqlstring}
)
SELECT z.zcta, z.hvi, z.geometry
FROM 'http://feeds/datasets/nyc-street-heat/zcta.parquet' z, s
WHERE z.hvi IS NOT NULL
  AND z.south < s.n + 0.005 AND z.north > s.s - 0.005 AND z.west < s.e + 0.005 AND z.east > s.w - 0.005

spec.description: Every building coloured by the Heat Vulnerability Index of the ZIP code it stands in (DOHMH, 1 lowest risk to 5 highest): surface temperature, green space, home air conditioning and the share of residents who are low-income or non-Latinx Black. One value per ZIP code: the street air above is what changes from block to block.
spec.title: Heat vulnerability, building by building

config.label: Heat Vulnerability Index of the ZIP code

spec.rawSql:
-- The neighbourhood's sensors over the ten days, hour by hour. The map's time filter keeps the brushed window
-- (t0, t1): each sensor's reading in it colours the buildings, and a building's card charts the whole range. Each
-- hourly mean stands at the middle of its hour, so a one-hour window holds exactly one.
SELECT sensor, mount, neighbourhood, latitude, longitude,
       time + INTERVAL 30 MINUTE AS time, temp_c
FROM 'http://feeds/datasets/nyc-street-heat/readings.parquet'
WHERE nta = ${nta:sqlstring}
ORDER BY time, sensor

spec.description: OpenStreetMap's buildings, each coloured by the air temperature estimated at its centre from the closest street sensors (inverse distance weighting), in the brushed hour. A building more than 250 m from every sensor stays grey. The dots are the sensors, in the colour of their own reading. Hover a building for its card: the estimate at that building over the ten days, the brushed hour as its value; pin the card to keep it. Pick another neighbourhood above and the map moves there.
spec.title: Every building, by the street air around it

spec.rawSql:
-- Every hour of the ten days in the neighbourhood: its coolest, mean and hottest sensor.
SELECT time, min(temp_c) AS "Coolest sensor", round(avg(temp_c), 1) AS "Mean",
       max(temp_c) AS "Hottest sensor"
FROM 'http://feeds/datasets/nyc-street-heat/readings.parquet'
WHERE nta = ${nta:sqlstring}
GROUP BY time ORDER BY time

spec.description: The neighbourhood's coolest, mean and hottest sensor every hour from 15 to 24 July 2019 (New York time). The band is the brushed window. The heat wave peaked on Saturday 20 and Sunday 21 July.
spec.title: The ten days, hour by hour

spec.rawSql:
-- The window's sensors in the neighbourhood: the hottest and the coolest, their mean,
-- and how many reported (each sensor's mean over the window).
WITH s AS (
  SELECT sensor, avg(temp_c) AS t FROM 'http://feeds/datasets/nyc-street-heat/readings.parquet'
  WHERE nta = ${nta:sqlstring} AND time >= (${t0:sqlstring}::TIMESTAMPTZ AT TIME ZONE 'UTC') AND time < (${t1:sqlstring}::TIMESTAMPTZ AT TIME ZONE 'UTC')
  GROUP BY sensor
)
SELECT round(max(t), 1) AS "Hottest", round(min(t), 1) AS "Coolest",
       round(max(t) - min(t), 1) AS "Spread", count(*) AS "Sensors"
FROM s

spec.description: The neighbourhood's hottest and coolest sensor over the brushed window, the spread between them (how much one block differs from the next), and how many sensors reported.
spec.title: Sensors in the hour

spec.rawSql:
-- The neighbourhood's sensors over the window, the hottest first.
SELECT sensor AS "Sensor", mount AS "On a", round(avg(temp_c), 1) AS "°C",
       round(avg(temp_f), 1) AS "°F"
FROM 'http://feeds/datasets/nyc-street-heat/readings.parquet'
WHERE nta = ${nta:sqlstring} AND time >= (${t0:sqlstring}::TIMESTAMPTZ AT TIME ZONE 'UTC') AND time < (${t1:sqlstring}::TIMESTAMPTZ AT TIME ZONE 'UTC')
GROUP BY sensor, mount
ORDER BY "°C" DESC

spec.description: The neighbourhood's sensors over the brushed window, the hottest first: on a street tree or a light pole.
spec.title: Each sensor in the hour
New York's street heat, block by block — the July 2019 heat wave

spec.definition:
-- The study's neighbourhoods with five sensors or more, the most first.
SELECT neighbourhood || ' (' || count(DISTINCT sensor) || ' sensors)' AS __text, nta AS __value
FROM 'http://feeds/datasets/nyc-street-heat/readings.parquet'
GROUP BY nta, neighbourhood
HAVING count(DISTINCT sensor) >= 5
ORDER BY count(DISTINCT sensor) DESC
spec.label: Neighbourhood
spec.name: nta
